svg.title: The Unfinished Library — two shelves of possibility
svg.desc: An illustrated bookshelf with dark wooden boards and alcoves, vivid covers, literary pun titles, closely packed and deliberately leaning books, curved and folding shelves joined to the case, Penrose and Hat tiling compartments, impossible triangles, cubes and tridents, stairways connected to shelf boards and miniature libraries inside archways. Potted ferns, flowers and trailing vines grow among tiny mice, toadstools, owls, toy houses, rocking horses, fishbowls and pendulum clocks. A finite, still vector keepsake from a webpage where fish swim, pendulums swing, toy horses rock, occasional leaves drift down and a few winged books wander through the shelves. Illustrative inspiration: Colin Thompson. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Thompson_(writer) Hat geometry: David Smith, Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig S. Kaplan and Chaim Goodman-Strauss. https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~csk/hat/
svg.metadata:
MATHEMATICAL SHELF CONSTRUCTION
The finite Hat polygon fixture in hat-tiles.js is derived from the initial H and P metatiles and their first attachment in the authors' Hatviz construction. Its six congruent Hat tiles include one reflected tile. The patch is stored as exact triangular-lattice coordinates and rendered with uniform scaling. It is a finite illustration of the construction, not an infinite tiling generated by this webpage. Checks confirmed equal tile areas, matching interior seams, no overlapping interiors, and a single exterior boundary with no interior holes.
Mathematical work: David Smith, Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig S. Kaplan, and Chaim Goodman-Strauss, "An aperiodic monotile" (2023; published 2024). Primary project page: https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~csk/hat/ Construction source: https://github.com/isohedral/hatviz Source files: geometry.js and hat.js, initial H/P definitions and constructPatch.
The following notice applies to the Hatviz-derived polygon fixture. The full notice is also retained in hat-tiles.js and therefore in the standalone page.
